subskill: Linear inequality model with a parameter: counting feasible whole-number quantities
prompt: A pottery studio charges a one-time registration fee of $35 plus k dollars for each class, where k is a positive integer. Mira will spend at most $180 in total, and she must sign up for at least 2 classes. There are exactly 3 different numbers of classes Mira could sign up for. For how many integer values of k is this true?
explanation: If Mira signs up for n classes, she pays 35 + kn dollars, so 35 + kn ≤ 180, which gives n ≤ 145/k. Together with n ≥ 2, the possible numbers of classes are 2, 3, ..., up to the greatest integer that is at most 145/k. Exactly 3 numbers means those are 2, 3 and 4, so 4 must be affordable and 5 must not be: 4 ≤ 145/k < 5. That gives 29 < k ≤ 36.25. At k = 29 she can afford exactly 5 classes (35 + 145 = 180 is allowed), which gives 4 choices, so 29 is excluded. The integer values are 30 through 36, which is 7 values. The option 9 leaves out the $35 fee and solves 4 ≤ 180/k < 5. The option 12 ignores the minimum of 2 classes, so it looks for 1, 2 and 3 classes and solves 3 ≤ 145/k < 4. The option 15 makes both of those errors.
mechanism: budget inequality with a per-unit parameter
minimum quantity shifts the count
boundary price where the next count becomes affordable

setup.i: k is the per-class price in a fee-plus-price budget model
setup.ii: exactly 3 possible whole-number class counts, with a minimum of 2 classes
setup.iii: number of integer values of k

solve: let c=0; for(let k=1;k<=500;k++){let opts=0; for(let n=2;n<=500;n++){ if(35+k*n<=180) opts++ } if(opts===3) c++ } return c

subskill: Linear inequality kx ≥ c on a finite set of integers: both signs of k
prompt:
For how many integer values of the constant k are exactly 4 of the integers from -6 through 9 solutions to the inequality below?
kx ≥ 36
explanation: k cannot be 0, since 0 ≥ 36 is false for every x. If k > 0, dividing by k keeps the direction: x ≥ 36/k. The solutions in the list are the integers from the smallest integer at least 36/k up to 9, and exactly 4 of them means they are 6, 7, 8, 9, so 5 < 36/k ≤ 6, which gives 6 ≤ k < 7.2: k = 6 or 7. If k < 0, dividing by k reverses the direction: x ≤ 36/k. The solutions are -6 up to the greatest integer at most 36/k, and exactly 4 means -6, -5, -4, -3, so -3 ≤ 36/k < -2. For negative k this gives -18 < k ≤ -12: k = -17, -16, -15, -14, -13, -12. At k = -18, 36/k = -2, so x ≤ -2 allows 5 integers and k = -18 is excluded. In all, 2 + 6 = 8 values. The option 2 counts only positive k (or divides by a negative k without reversing the inequality, which leaves no negative k that works). The option 7 treats kx ≥ 36 as kx > 36, which moves every boundary and gives k = 7 and k = -18 through -13. The option 20 counts the integers from -6 to n as n + 6 instead of n + 7 in the negative case, which shifts that range to -35 through -18.
mechanism: sign of k decides the direction
negative k reverses the inequality
attained versus excluded boundary of k

setup.i: k multiplies x; x ranges over a fixed set of integers spanning negative and positive values
setup.ii: exactly 4 integers in the set satisfy the inequality
setup.iii: number of integer values of k

solve: let c=0; for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){let m=0; for(let x=-6;x<=9;x++){ if(k*x>=36) m++ } if(m===4) c++ } return c

subskill: System of linear inequalities with a parameter: sum of integer solutions fixed
prompt:
4 - 3x ≤ 22
4x < k - 30
In the system of inequalities above, k is a constant. The integer solutions of the system have a sum of -18. What is the sum of all integer values of k for which this is true?
explanation: The first inequality gives -3x ≤ 18, so x ≥ -6 (dividing by -3 reverses the inequality). The second gives x < (k - 30)/4. So the integer solutions are -6, -5, ..., m, where m is the greatest integer less than (k - 30)/4. Their sum is -18 in two ways: -6 + (-5) + (-4) + (-3) = -18 (m = -3), and -6 + (-5) + ... + 1 + 2 = -18 (m = 2), because the terms from -2 to 2 add to 0. For m = -3: -3 < (k - 30)/4 ≤ -2, so 18 < k ≤ 22, giving k = 19, 20, 21, 22 (sum 82). At k = 22, x < -2 still allows -3, so k = 22 counts. For m = 2: 2 < (k - 30)/4 ≤ 3, so 38 < k ≤ 42, giving k = 39, 40, 41, 42 (sum 162). The total is 82 + 162 = 244. The option 162 finds only the stopping point m = 2 and misses that the solutions can also stop at -3. The option 180 finds both but excludes k = 22 and k = 42, treating (k - 30)/4 = -2 or 3 as though it allowed one more solution. The option 236 treats 4x < k - 30 as 4x ≤ k - 30, which includes k = 18 and k = 38 and excludes k = 22 and k = 42 (k = 18 through 21 and 38 through 41).
mechanism: strict bound on x set by k
two different solution sets give the same sum
included versus excluded boundary of k

setup.i: k in the constant of the strict upper bound; the other inequality (after a flip) fixes an attained negative lower bound
setup.ii: the integer solutions sum to a given negative number
setup.iii: sum of all integer values of k

distractor_solve.162: let s=0; for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){ let sum=0, n=0, top=-999; for(let x=-300;x<=300;x++){ if(4-3*x<=22 && 4*x<k-30){ sum+=x; n++; top=x } } if(n>0 && sum===-18 && top>0) s+=k } return s

subskill: Linear inequality with the parameter in the x-coefficient: number of positive integer solutions
prompt: Exactly 5 positive integers x make the inequality kx ≤ 3x + 2k + 114 true, where k is a constant. If m and M are the least and greatest integer values of k that allow this, what is M - m?
explanation: Rewrite the inequality as (k - 3)x ≤ 2k + 114. If k = 3, it reads 0 ≤ 120, true for every x. If k < 3, dividing by the negative number k - 3 reverses it: x ≥ (2k + 114)/(k - 3), which every large enough positive integer satisfies, so there are infinitely many solutions. So k > 3, and x ≤ (2k + 114)/(k - 3) = 2 + 120/(k - 3). Exactly 5 positive solutions means x = 1, ..., 5 work and x = 6 does not: 5 ≤ 2 + 120/(k - 3) < 6, so 3 ≤ 120/(k - 3) < 4, which gives 30 < k - 3 ≤ 40, or 33 < k ≤ 43. The integer values are 34 through 43, so M - m = 43 - 34 = 9. The option 3 drops the 2 when dividing and solves 5 ≤ 120/(k - 3) < 6 (k = 24 through 27). The option 19 counts 0 as one of the five solutions, so it allows only x = 1 through 4 (k = 44 through 63). The option 39 requires only that x = 5 work and never checks that x = 6 fails (k = 4 through 43).
mechanism: sign of the x-coefficient k - 3
reversing the inequality when k - 3 < 0 gives infinitely many solutions
both x = 5 included and x = 6 excluded

setup.i: k in both the x-coefficient and the constant of one inequality (x-coefficient k - 3)
setup.iii: difference between the greatest and least integer values of k

solve: const ks=[]; for(let k=-300;k<=300;k++){ let m=0; for(let x=1;x<=3000;x++){ if(k*x<=3*x+2*k+114) m++ } if(m===5) ks.push(k) } return Math.max(...ks)-Math.min(...ks)

subskill: Compound linear inequality with the parameter multiplying x: both signs of k
prompt:
-4 ≤ kx ≤ 45
For a nonzero constant k, exactly 3 integers x satisfy the compound inequality above. What is the difference between the greatest and least integer values of k for which this is true?
explanation: x = 0 always satisfies the inequality. If k > 0, dividing by k gives -4/k ≤ x ≤ 45/k. Exactly 3 integers means the solutions are 0, 1, 2, so 2 ≤ 45/k < 3 and -1 < -4/k. The first gives 15 < k ≤ 22.5, and for those k the second holds too, so k = 16 through 22. If k < 0, dividing by k reverses both inequalities: 45/k ≤ x ≤ -4/k. Now the solutions must be -2, -1, 0, so -3 < 45/k ≤ -2, which for negative k gives -22.5 ≤ k < -15: k = -22 through -16. The greatest integer value is 22 and the least is -22, so the difference is 44. The option 6 uses only positive k (22 - 16), which is what results from not reversing the inequalities for negative k: the bounds come out in the wrong order and no negative k seems to work. The option 30 forgets that 0 is a solution and looks for three nonzero solutions, giving k from -15 to 15. The option 3 makes both of those errors (15 - 12).
mechanism: dividing by a negative k reverses both parts
x = 0 is always a solution
positive and negative k ranges are separate

setup.i: k multiplies the middle of a compound inequality whose ends are constants
setup.iii: difference between the greatest and least integer values of k

subskill: Linear function from a table compared with a parameter on a finite set of integers
prompt:
The table shows three values of the linear function f.
x | f(x)
-2 | 29
0 | 23
4 | 11
For exactly 6 of the integers x from -3 through 10, f(x) ≥ k, where k is a constant. What is the greatest integer value of k?
explanation: From the table, f decreases by 6 when x increases by 2, so the slope is -3 and f(x) = 23 - 3x. Then 23 - 3x ≥ k gives -3x ≥ k - 23, and dividing by -3 reverses the inequality: x ≤ (23 - k)/3. So the solutions in the list are -3, -2, ..., up to the greatest integer at most (23 - k)/3. Exactly 6 of them means -3 through 2, so 2 ≤ (23 - k)/3 < 3, which gives 14 < k ≤ 17. At k = 17, x ≤ 2 exactly, so 2 is still a solution. The greatest integer value of k is 17. The option 10 does not reverse the inequality and counts down from 10 using x ≥ (23 - k)/3. The option 8 counts only the integers from 0 through 10, leaving out -3, -2 and -1. The option 31 reverses the inequality but does not change the sign of k - 23 when dividing by -3, using x ≤ (k - 23)/3.
mechanism: slope read from a table
dividing by -3 reverses the inequality
negative integers in the set count

setup.i: k is the constant compared with a decreasing linear function given by a table; x ranges over a fixed set of integers
setup.ii: exactly 6 integers in the set satisfy the inequality

solve: const slope=(11-29)/(4-(-2)), b=23; let best=-1e9; for(let k=-300;k<=300;k++){ let m=0; for(let x=-3;x<=10;x++){ if(b+slope*x>=k) m++ } if(m===6) best=Math.max(best,k) } return best

subskill: Compound inequality with the parameter at both ends: greatest parameter for a fixed integer count
prompt:
k + 1 ≤ x < 3k
Exactly 5 integers x satisfy the compound inequality above, where k is a constant. What is the greatest possible value of k?
explanation: The solutions are the integers x with k + 1 ≤ x < 3k. Try k = 10/3: the inequality is 13/3 ≤ x < 10, whose integer solutions are 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, exactly 5. The right end is exactly 10, and x < 10 excludes 10, so the strict inequality is what keeps the count at 5. Now take any k greater than 10/3. If k ≤ 4, the left end k + 1 is at most 5 and the right end 3k is greater than 10, so 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are all solutions: at least 6. If k > 4, the interval has length 3k - (k + 1) = 2k - 1 > 7, so it contains at least 7 integers. Either way there are more than 5 solutions, so the greatest possible value of k is 10/3. The option 4 uses only the left-end condition k + 1 ≤ 5 and never checks the right end. The option 11/3 counts 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 as five integers (10 - 5 = 5) and so lets 3k go up to 11. The option 7/2 requires only that the length 3k - (k + 1) = 2k - 1 be at most 6, ignoring where the ends fall.
mechanism: both ends depend on k at different rates
strict right end attained at the boundary value
checking both ends rather than the length

setup.i: k in both ends of a compound inequality with different multipliers
setup.iii: greatest possible value of k (k need not be an integer)

solve: let best=-1e9; for(let i=0;i<=6000;i++){ const k=i/600; let m=0; for(let x=-50;x<=50;x++){ if(k+1<=x && x<3*k) m++ } if(m===5) best=Math.max(best,k) } return best

subskill: System of linear inequalities with the parameter in both bounds: no integer solution
prompt:
k - 2x < -3
5x ≤ 2k + 30
What is the least integer value of the constant k for which no integer x satisfies both inequalities above?
explanation: The first inequality gives -2x < -k - 3, so x > (k + 3)/2 (dividing by -2 reverses it). The second gives x ≤ (2k + 30)/5. The solutions form the interval (k + 3)/2 < x ≤ (2k + 30)/5, whose length is (2k + 30)/5 - (k + 3)/2 = (45 - k)/10. When k ≤ 35 the length is at least 1, and an interval of this kind with length at least 1 always contains an integer. For k = 36 the interval is 19.5 < x ≤ 20.4, which contains 20. For k = 37 it is 20 < x ≤ 20.8: x = 20 is excluded by the strict inequality and 21 is too large, so there is no integer solution. The least integer value of k is 37. The option 45 only looks for when the interval itself becomes empty, (k + 3)/2 ≥ (2k + 30)/5. The option 42 treats the first inequality as x ≥ (k + 3)/2, so x = 20 would still work at k = 37. The option 35 treats the second inequality as x < (2k + 30)/5, which removes x = 20 at k = 35 (where the interval would be 19 < x < 20).
mechanism: two bounds that move with k at different rates
empty of integers before the interval is empty
strict versus non-strict at each end

setup.i: k in both inequalities of a system, with the bounds moving at different rates
